rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while maximizing the chance of observing all 10 compounds. A middle temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

All pairs have resolution to spare, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty. Keeping the window and temperature fixed will reveal which critical pairs lose resolution as the gradient steepens.

The shorter gradient eliminates the time penalty but compresses a critical cluster. Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test whether temperature-dependent selectivity separates that cluster without extending the run.

Use an intermediate temperature to avoid the near-coelution seen at 60 C, with a slightly shallower gradient to recover separation in the central cluster. The last peak should remain near the time-penalty-free window.

Test 55 C to balance separation of the central cluster against the different pair that nearly coelutes at 60 C. Returning to the 10-minute gradient may improve the temperature-sensitive pair while keeping the time penalty at zero.

Lengthen the best method's gradient slightly to improve the remaining under-resolved pair. The last peak should still elute before the time penalty begins, giving a chance to reach full resolution without sacrificing speed.

Injection 6 already reached the maximum possible CRF. This shorter gradient preserves its slope and temperature through the entire observed elution window, so it should retain full separation and zero time penalty with a lower final organic fraction.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a further-trimmed endpoint with the same successful gradient slope. All observed peaks should still elute during the gradient, preserving separation while reducing the final organic fraction.

With the maximum score secured, test whether shifting the gradient window upward at the same slope shortens elution while retaining full resolution. This probes sensitivity to the starting composition rather than repeating an equivalent gradient.

Slightly reduce the slope at the higher starting composition to recover the pair that lost resolution in injection 9. This may retain the maximum CRF while giving more balanced critical-pair separations and a last-peak time below 8 minutes.

Reduce the slope from 0.06875 to 0.065 organic fraction per minute to lift the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. Extrapolation from injections 9–10 suggests the last peak will still elute before 8 minutes, potentially restoring CRF 1.000.

The maximum CRF is already secured; slightly flatten injection 11's gradient to test for greater critical-pair resolution margins. The last peak is predicted near 8 minutes, so this probes the boundary between full separation and the onset of a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already secured at 55 C. Explore the untested low-temperature limit with the short gradient to determine whether a different elution order offers another fully resolved, fast method.

With CRF 1.000 already secured, test a faster, high-temperature alternative. A substantially steeper gradient may move the near-coeluting pair at 60 C past its selectivity crossover, though other pairs may lose resolution.
